Geophys. J. R. astr. SOC. (1981) 65,493-503 
Palaeomagnetism of a Pan-African diorite: a Late 
Precambrian pole for western Africa 
* P. Morel 
34 06 0 Mon tpellier Cedex, France 
Centre Giologique et Geophysique, USTL, Place Eu'ugPne Bataillon, 
Received 1980 July 18; in original form 1980 February 29 
Summary. A study of a Late Pan-African diorite (Adma diorite; 18.3"N, 
1.2" E) gives a mean direction of magnetization D= 317.3", I= 78.6" (13 
sites, 62 samples, ag5 = 9.0") based on alternating field and thermal cleaning. 
The corresponding palaeopole is at 32.5" N, 344.7" E (Ag5 = 15.9"). The 
diorite is dated by UjPb method at 616 ? 11 Myr. The age of this magnetiza- 
tion is believed to be somewhat younger, between 590 and 616 Myr. 
Thermal treatment shows that above 675°C (Curie point of synthetic 
hematite and the hghest value usually observed in rocks) the specimens retain 
a magnetization whose intensity and direction are approximately the same 
across the collection. In some specimens, the directions continue to change 
between 670 and 720°C. The carrier of this 'high-temperature' magnetiza- 
tion is not known; it could be hematite with blocking temperature higher 
than 675"C, or iron, or an iron-rich mineral such as sphene. Comparison of 
the palaeopole with others from rocks of about the same age from Gondwana 
shows a good agreement. There is an excellent agreement with a result from 
southern Africa (Ntonya Ring Structure) which suggests that there have been 
no important motions between the different blocks which form Africa, at 
least since that time. This pole places western Africa in high latitudes and is 
consistent with the presence of upper Precambrian tillites. 
In order to add to the knowledge of the Late Precambrian geomagnetic Earth's field in 
Africa, the following study of a Pan-African dioritic intrusion from northern Mali is 
presented. 
Geology and sampling 
The Pan-African Orogeny was defined by Kennedy (1964) as a major African thermotec- 
tonic event that occurred about 550 Myr ago. Since then, deformations and intrusions of 
*Present address: Earth Physics Branch, Energy, Mines and Resources, Ottawa, Ontario KIA OY3, 
Canada.

this age have been recognized in South America, Australia, Antarctica and Europe. The Pan- 
African is represented in West Africa by the Hoggar and Nigerian shields (Fig. 1) and for a 
long time it was considered to be an intra-continental event. However, more recently it has 
been suggested that the Pan-African foldbelts of West Africa are probably caused by the 
approach and the collision of older nucleii (Black 1967, 1978; Caby 1970, 1978; Bayer & 
Lesquer 1978; Black etal. 1979a, b; Bertrand & Caby 1978; Bertrand etal. 1981). 
The Adrar des Iforas of northern Mali (Fig. 1) is part of the Pharusian belt as defined by 
Bertrand & Caby (1978). The Adrar des Iforas is characterized by several tectono-strati- 
graphic units and events (Bertrand & Caby 1978; Black 1978; Boullier et al. 1978; Caby 
1978; Bertrand et al. 1981 ; Black ecal. 1979): 
The intrusion studied (Adma diorite) is a syn- to late-tectonic Pan-African intrusion. It 
is composed of diorite dated at 616 & 11 Myr, and adamellite dated at 613 f 3 Myr 
(method: U/Pb on zircons (Ducrot, Lancelot & Renaud, private communication)). It 
intrudes the ‘Srie de TafCliant’ as described by Fabre (1976). The Adma diorite can be 
taken to date the end of the Pan-African event at 620 & 30 Myr. A few results from a post 
Pan-African rhyolite (Tabankort rhyolite) are also given. 
Fifteen sites were drilled and seven sites hand-sampled. The sites were distributed over the 
intrusion (Fig. 2). Thirteen sites were taken from the diorite, three near to the contact with 
the ‘SCrie de TafCliant’, one (17) from the ‘SCrie de TafCliant’, itself metamorphosed at the 
contact by the diorite, one (14) from a post-diorite basic dyke, three (7, 8,9) in the contact 
area between the diorite and the adamellite and one (10) from the adamellite itself. Usually 
four or five cores or hand samples were taken at each site. Orientation was obtained by both 
magnetic and Sun compasses. The cores (2.54 cm diameter) were cut into 2.4 cm length 
cylinders, and the hand samples into cubes of 3.5 cm side. 
Results 
The measurements were made at the geomagnetic laboratory of Parc Saint-Maur (Paris, 
France). Magnetizations were measured with a translation inductometer (Daly 1970). 
Alternating field (af) treatments were performed in fields up to 160 mT using a three-axis 
tumbler. Thermal treatment was performed with a furnace controlled by two thermocouples. 
Heating was automatic and was carried out during the night to minimize external effects. AU 
treatments were carried out in a quasi-zero residual field (? 20 nT) provided by Helmholtz 
coils. Further details are given in Morel-A-1’Huissier (1978). 
Natural remanent magnetizations (NRM) of 189 cylinders from the cores and 25 cubes 
from the hand samples were measured after the samples had first been stored for one month 
in quasi-zero field to eliminate the principal part of the viscous remanent magnetization 
(VRM). The distribution is random and it seems reasonable to relate this dispersion to 
lightning (Rmbert 1958) which is very common in the sampling area. The within-site 
magnetization intensities are variable (ranging over the intrusion from 74 700 to 36 x 
A m-’). An experiment of ‘trainage’ was carried out in the Earth’s field over a period 
of one month. The change in the magnetization was less than 1 per cent in over 90 per cent 
of the samples. Evidently the natural remanence is stable on a short time-scale and 
essentially random in direction, but it surely does not reflect the primary magnetization of 
the diorite. 
Except for site 2, at least one specimen per site was treated in detail by thermal or af 
cleaning. For sites 1,4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11 and 22, two specimens from the same core were 
treated, one thermally and the other by alternating fields. For sites 5, 6, 11 and 22, the 
specimen treated by af was subsequently treated thermally between 670 and 720°C. A total

### page_4
49 6 P. Morel 
of 36 pilot specimens were studied. Fig. 3 illustrates the changes obtained using the different 
procedures. 
Af analysis (Fig. 3) shows that after 5 mT most of the specimens have lost about 50 per 
cent of their magnetization or more; the exceptions are discussed below. The major changes 
in direction occur between 0 and 40mT. After 40mT, there is a stabilization of the 
magnetization in both direction and intensity. Between 40 and 80mT (or 140mT 
depending on the maximum field applied), the magnetization intensity range is 50 to 5 x 
1 0-3 A m-' with a mean about 35 x A m-'. The intensity after final treatment usually 
represents only 1 to 10 per cent of the initial value. Fig. 3 also shows that after treatment in 
relatively weak fields (5 to 10mT) the specimens whose NRM was negatively inclined 
quickly change to a well-pronounced positive inclination. 
Some specimens behave differently (Fig. 3b). Their intensity after af treatment falls to 
only 60-70 per cent of the initial value, but the absolute remaining intensity is of the same 
magnitude as that for the other specimens. The final direction is also consistent with the 
others. Some specimens show also a small change in direction at the beginning of the treat- 
ment prior to the stabilization in direction which remains constant up to 140 mT. 
From this af study one can conclude that an important fraction of the magnetization

Palaeomagnetism of a Pan-African diorite 49 7 
('soft' magnetization) is carried by grains with weak blocking fields so that it is very sensitive 
to external field variations (especially to lightning) and is probably of recent origin. There is 
also a smaller part of the magnetization ('hard' magnetization) characterized by hgh 
blocking fields. Study of polished sections shows that the carrier of the 'soft' magnetization 
is probably a titanomagnetite. It occurs as large grains, more-or-less martitized, and often 
associated with ilmenite (Morel-a-1'Huissier 1978). The carrier of the 'hard' magnetization is 
probably hematite. 
The grouping of the directions and the presence of good 'stable end points', might lead to 
satisfaction with this af treatment, but the field that created the superimposed magnetiza- 
tion by lightning may have affected the hematite which is the presumed carrier of the 'hard' 
magnetization. If it has, af demagnetization does not permit adequate separation because the 
peak intensity of the af used could be less than the field produced by lightning very near to 
the impact point. 
In order to complete the analysis, thermal treatment was carried out (Fig. 3), step-by- 
step demagnetization up to 710 or 720°C for some specimens. The demagnetization curves 
show that the magnetization is carried by grains with a wide range of blocking temperature 
and size. First, there is a drop in intensity between 250 and 300"C, but it has not been 
possible to relate the magnetization removed during this interval to a component consistent in 
direction across the collection. The major drop occurs in the range 540-580°C and confirms 
the presence of magnetite (or somewhat titaniferous magnetite). Very often this drop is 
accompanied by a rapid change in direction. The small change in direction between 20 and 
540"C, the rapid change between 540 and 580°C and the relative stable direction between 
580 and 710°C (or 720°C) are shown in Fig. 3(c). Fig. 3(a, b) show two different sorts of 
behaviour. In 3(a) there is little change in direction between 20 and 720°C and in 3(b) 
there is a continuous evolution of the direction between 20 and 580°C followed by a quasi- 
stable direction. Generally (Fig. 3a, c), below 580°C the intensity represents 10 to 20 per 
cent of the initial value, and above 580°C (as for af demagnetization) the remaining 
magnetization represents no more than 1 to 10 per cent (average between 1 and 5 per cent) 
of the initial intensity. Sometimes, it is also possible to observe a comparable evolution of 
the direction above 580°C and up to 675"C, the Curie point of synthetic hematite. At this 
stage, the decrease in intensity ceases and, in the interval up to 720"C, the direction 
fluctuates around a mean position. 
As a further test and because the af peak intensity could be lower than the intensity 
produced by lightning, some specimens were first treated in af fields up to 140 mT and then 
thermally demagnetized. Four specimens were chosen and the thermal treatment was then 
carried out between 670 and 720°C. Specimen 6-2 is an example (Fig. 3b). After 670°C 
there is a systematic small decrease in intensity sometimes accompanied by a change in 
direction whch also indicates that the hematite may have been partially remagnetized by 
lightning. Another possible explanation whch is partly supported by Fig. 3(b) could be that 
both polarities are present in some specimens. One can asgue&t the negative polarity is 
never found, but if we consider two polarities with very similar blocking temperatures or 
blocking fields, it becomes rather impossible, with existing techniques, to separate them. 
In fact, we only obtain the resultant vector which could be more-or-less near the direction of 
one polarity depending on the difference between the intensities of the two moments. From 
680 to 720°C the direction fluctuates around a mean position and, in general, the directions 
found after thermal treatment are not far from those obtained after af treatment at 140 mT 
(which is almost stable since 40 mT). 
Based on these detailed studies, the rest of the collection was treated in the following 
way: (1) af demagnetization at 80mT, (2) measurement, (3) heating at 710"C, and (4)

### page_6
49 8 P. Morel 
measurement again. A total of 1 17 specimens (pilot specimens included) from 22 sites were 
treated in this manner. 
These do not represent all the samples collected. Unfortunately the time available to 
process the specimens was limited and a choice had to be made between processing all the 
samples in less detail or a selection of them in greater detail. The latter procedure seemed 
more reasonable since the 11 7 specimens treated are undoubtedly representative of the in- 
trusion as a whole. 
After thermal treatment at 710°C the remaining magnetization is systematic in direction. 
This is unusual because the Curie temperature of synthetic hematite is = 675°C. The effect 
is not related to poor temperature control because two thermocouples agreed to k2"C. 
It is not caused by poor cancellation of the field; this was checked by carrying out duplicate 
heatings at the same temperature (710"C), inverting the specimens between the runs and 
showing that the direction after the second run remained the same. A further experiment 
was carried out with a specimen of synthetic hematite which was given a thermoremanent 
magnetization (TRM) by heating at 800°C and cooling in the Earth's field. This specimen 
was demagnetized along with the rock specimens. At 680°C the rock specimens retained a 
non-negligible magnetization, whereas the specimen of synthetic hematite had lost all its 
magnetization. Thus, the magnetization persisting at high temperature is not caused by 
experimental error and apparently has a blocking temperature between 680 and 800°C. 
But what is the carrier of such a magnetization? It could be hematite. Smith & Fuller 
(1967) mention that the magnetization of hematite consists of a soft spin-canted moment 
observed in the range -20 to 675°C and a hard defect moment lost at the true NBel point 
of hematite (725°C). On the other hand, Park (1975, 1977) on experimental grounds notes 
the possibility of a higher Curie point for hematite. If the magnetization is related to 
hematite, it is probably not a TRM but more likely a chemical remanent magnetization 
(CRM), because polished sections show that hematite was formed during late-plutonic 
autometamorphism whch probably occurred at temperatures below the Curie point of 
hematite. Other possibilities are native iron (this was not observed in polished sections) or 
sphene which can contain up to 15 per cent of iron in the form Fe,03, which is abundant in 
these rocks and often associated with magnetic minerals (Morel-WHuissier 1978).

average of the two values was used for calculations of the overall mean values. Fig. 4 shows

the results obtained for the 13 sites used in the final calculations (sites 1, 3 to 13 and 20). 
Results from nine sites have not been used for the following reasons: site 14 is a post- 
diorite dyke; sites 15, 21 and 22 have internally random distribution of directions even after 
magnetic and thermal cleaning; the directions at sites 2 and 19 agree with the direction at 
the 13 sites used but have not been included because they are based on two specimens only; 
site 16 gives a very different mean direction; sites 17 and 18 sampled at the 'SCrie de 
Tafbliant' - diorite contact give also a different mean direction. It is noteworthy that site 
19 sampled 100 m from 17 and 18 give a direction (D = 137", I= 53") that is consistent 
with the mean direction. The argument of the presence of two polarities can also be used to 
explain the dispersion with sites 15, 16, 17, 18, 21 and 22. At these sites, both polarities 
could be present with a more-or-less equal intensity, and if these polarities are slightly 
misaligned (because of secular variation), they could produce a nearly horizontal resultant 
vector (Table 1). Fig. 4(a) shows the NRM of all the specimens treated from the 13 sites. 
Fig. 4(b, c) show the results from each core (results from sites 2 and 19 included) and from 
each site. The effect of cleaning plus the averaging of specimens from the same core is seen 
by comparing Fig. 4(a, b). The effect of averaging from cores to sites is seen by comparing 
Fig. J(b, c). The mean of all cores (D = 301.7", I= 86.1", N= 62, agS = 6.1") is not signifi- 
cantly different from the mean (D = 3 17.3", I = 78.6", N = 13, ag5 = 9.0" ) calculated from

the sites (Fig. 4c and Table 2). In Table 2, the palaeopole is calculated in three different 
ways from the mean of cores, from the mean of sites and by averaging the virtual 
geomagnetic poles (VCPs) for each site. The results are very close. They are also in excellent 
agreement with the mean calculated after af treatment at 80 mT (D = 3 11.2", I = 80.5", 
N=51, ag5= 7.1" giving cores unit weight;D=319.8",1=77.5",N= 11,ag5= 10.8" giving 
sites unit weight). As the intrusion did not cool instantaneously, but rather over a long 
period, it seems reasonable to assume that the magnetization at each site is uniform and 
records the geomagnetic field for a given time that is short compared to the cooling interval 
spanned by all the sites from the intrusion. Therefore, the preferred summary value is line 3 
of Table 2 in whch the mean of the VGPs has been obtained by treating the specimens first 
at 80 mT and secondly at 710°C. 
It seems probable that the stable high-temperature magnetization is caused by hematite 
which is a product of chemical changes during late plutonic autometamorphism. If this is 
correct, the time at which this process ceased will be the age of the magnetization. The time 
at which this alteration ceased is probably between the time of intrusion of the diorite 
(616 k 11 Myr) and the intrusion of the late stage ring complexes (590Myr, Ducrot et al., 
private communication). The latter are the final igneous events in this region and mark the 
time when the region finally cooled after the Pan-African Orogeny. According to this argu- 
ment, the magnetization is in the age limits 616-590Myr, and thls seems to be the most 
reasonable choice. 
Preliminary results from the Tabankort rhyolite support this opinion. The Tabankort 
rhyolite (19.7" N, 1.1" E) made up of a succession of green and red flows is also from the 
Adrar des Iforas but north of the Adma diorite. The rhyolite overlies the intrusive suite of 
which the Adma diorite is a part and which is considered to be equivalent to some nearby 
granitic intrusions that yield a zircon age of about 590 Myr (Ducrot et al., private communi- 
cation). This preliminary study is based on eight specimens from three sub-horizontal lava 
flows. Af demagnetization up to 140mT and thermal demagnetization up to 715°C were 
done. These specimens give a mean direction D = 114", I= - 70" (ag5 = 7") and the 
corresponding palaeopole is 30" N, 322" E (dm = 12", dp = 10"). This palaeopole is in good 
agreement with that from the diorite, but the direction is reversed. This agreement between 
such different rock types is good evidence in support of the conclusion that the age of the 
palaeopole from the Adma diorite is about 590 Myr. 
Discussion 
Fig. 5 shows other palaeopoles from Gondwana from rocks of similar age to the Adma 
diorite. There is a good agreement between these poles, and specially notable is the agree- 
ment between the Adma diorite palaeopole (AD) and the Ntonya Ring Structure palaeopole 
(NRS) the latter body being dated at 630 +_ 24 Myr. This shows for the first time from well-

Figure 5. Late Precambrian-Lower Cambrian palaeopoles for Gondwana. NRS Ntonya Ring Structure; 
SG Sijarira Group; DM Deza Mountain; KF Klipheuvel Formation; AD Adma diorite; TR Tabankort 
rhyolite; ER Edith River; APB Antrim Plateau basalts; RBA red beds of Argentina. ER and APB are 
corrected using the reconstruction of Smith & Hallam (1970); RBA is corrected using the reconstruction 
of Bullard, Everett & Smith (1965). 1 and 2 are respectively the sampling localities of AD and NRS. 
dated rock units that the southern and the western part of Africa have probably kept their 
actual relative position at least since this period. But, because of its post-tectonic origin, 
this result does not corroborate or nullify the hypothesis that the Pan-African foldbelt is a 
collision Orogeny. Perhaps, as the systematic dating program of the Adrar des Iforas 
proceeds, it will be possible to find a suitable older material (= 700 Myr) to study this 
question by palaeomagnetic means. 
If we consider the Tabankort rhyolite, it seems that the pole moves westward from the 
west African coast. This supports the hypothesis of McElhinny, Giddings & Embleton 
(1974) and Veevers & McElhinny (1976) of a polar migration from south-eastern Gondwana 
to north-western Gondwana, placing Africa during the Late Precambrian in high latitudes 
r \ \ \ 1 1 1 
Figure 6. Palaeolatitude map for Africa. G occurrences for late Precambrian glaciation, their approximate 
ages are from Kroner (1977) and given in 106yr.

### page_10
502 P. Morel 
(Fig. 6) in opposition to Piper’s (1973) conclusions. Palaeolatitudes of Fig. 6 have been 
derived from the Adma diorite palaeopole and do not necessarily correlate with the oldest 
glacial occurrences shown in the figure. The results presented here tell us nothing about the 
problem of the non-synchroneity (Kroner 1977) or the diachronism (Deynoux et al. 1978) 
of Late Precambrian glaciations, but it is interesting to mention that the proposed 
correlation of Kroner (1977, p. 293) for the last glaciation of the Late Precambrian seems to 
be in excellent agreement with a polar migration (1 725 Myr for the Numees Formation and 
Chuos Formation of southern Africa to 1600 Myr for the Taoudeni basin, Mauritania, 
Fig. 6). Though this palaeopole needs corroboration by other African studies, it disagrees 
with the palaeomagnetic reconstruction proposed by Morel & Irving (1978) for the Pre- 
cambrian-Cambrian boundary. That reconstruction was in good agreement with Piper’s 
(1 973) interpretation which has been supported by Williams (1 974, 1975) and discussed by 
Kroner (1977). The existence or non-existence of Gondwana prior to Late Precambrian 
times cannot be established from the palaeomagnetic data presently available. This is mainly 
because of the poor age control of most of the palaeopoles, especially for those from 
Australia and South America.
